explain.title: Atomic number
explain.body: The number of protons present in the atoms of an element is always fixed and it is called the atomic number of that element. It is represented by Z. An element is identified by its atomic number.

explain.title: Mass number
explain.body: The total number of protons and neutrons present in an atom almost accounts for the total mass of that atom and hence it is called its nucleon number or mass number. It is represented by A. The mass of electron being very small is not included in the mass number.

explain.title: Reading an atom symbol
explain.body: The atomic number is written as a left subscript while the mass number as a left superscript. For example, ¹⁶₈O has 8 protons and a mass number of 16.

explain.title: Finding neutrons
explain.body: The number of neutrons N present in an atom can be calculated if its atomic number Z and mass number (A) are known. N = A − Z. Since an atom as a whole is electrically neutral, the number of electrons equals the number of protons.

mistakes: Do not mix up the left superscript A (mass number) and left subscript Z (atomic number).
Do not use A + Z to find neutrons; use N = A − Z.
Do not say that the mass number includes electrons; it counts protons and neutrons.
For a neutral atom, do not make the electron count equal to the mass number; it equals the proton count.

explain.title: What are isotopes?
explain.body: “Atoms of the same element having different number of neutrons in their nuclei are called isotopes.” Isotopes have the same atomic number but can have different mass numbers.

explain.title: Why are their properties alike and different?
explain.body: “Since the chemical properties of the elements are determined by the number of electrons, all three isotopes will show almost the same chemical behaviour, although their physical properties may be different.” Their different neutron numbers mean different masses.

explain.title: Radioactivity and radioactive decay
explain.body: “This process of emission of radiation is called radioactivity and the isotope which emits energy is called radioactive isotope.” When a radioactive element emits radiation and changes into another element, the process is called radioactive decay.

explain.title: Uses of radioactive isotopes
explain.body: They are used for medical imaging and diagnosing or treating disease. Carbon-14 is used to estimate the age of organic material. Radioactive isotopes can also be used to test the strength of metals and concrete mixtures.

explain.title: Ionization by radiation
explain.body: Radiation with enough energy can force one or more electrons away from an atom. Since the atom loses negative charge, it becomes a positively charged ion called a cation.

mistakes: Do not confuse atomic number with mass number: neutrons = mass number − atomic number.
Do not say isotopes have different numbers of protons; isotopes of one element have the same atomic number.

explain.title: Why relative atomic mass is useful
explain.body: Atoms of different elements have different masses. A common reference scale lets us compare them and helps us work out the ratios in which reactants combine.

explain.title: Isotope abundances make a weighted average

explain.title: The atom and its nucleus
explain.body: An atom has a very small nucleus containing protons and neutrons. Electrons are arranged around the nucleus in shells. Almost all the atom's mass is in the nucleus because electrons have very little mass.

explain.title: Atomic number and neutron number
explain.body: The number of protons is the atomic number and identifies the element. In a neutral atom, the number of electrons equals the number of protons. Number of neutrons = mass number − atomic number.

explain.title: Electron shells and energy
explain.body: Electrons in shells farther from the nucleus have greater energy. An atom absorbs energy when an electron moves to a higher energy shell and evolves or releases energy when an electron moves to a lower energy shell.

explain.title: Isotopes and relative atomic mass
explain.body: Isotopes are atoms of the same element with the same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons. Their relative atomic mass is a weighted mean based on the abundance of each isotope.

explain.title: Radioactivity and its uses
explain.body: Radioactivity is the spontaneous emission of radiation from an unstable nucleus. Radioactive isotopes have uses such as treating cancer, estimating the age of organic matter, and acting as tracers.

Do not say isotopes have different numbers of protons. They have the same proton number and different neutron numbers.

When explaining energy absorption, say that the electron moves to a higher energy shell; emission occurs when it moves to a lower energy shell.

notes.title: Atomic Number and Mass Number
notes.answer: Atomic number Z is the number of protons. Mass number A is the total number of protons and neutrons. Neutrons N = A − Z; electrons equal protons in a neutral atom.
notes.explanation: An element is identified by its atomic number, Z, which tells us how many protons its atoms have. The mass number, A, is the total number of protons and neutrons. Subtract Z from A to find the number of neutrons. In a neutral atom, electrons equal protons. For example, ¹⁶₈O has 8 protons, 8 electrons and 8 neutrons; ³²₁₆S has 16 neutrons.
notes.simple: The atomic number gives the protons. The mass number gives protons plus neutrons. Subtract to find neutrons; in a neutral atom, electrons equal protons.
steps: Read the left subscript: Z = number of protons.
For a neutral atom, set the number of electrons equal to the number of protons.
Read the left superscript: A = mass number.
Calculate neutrons using N = A − Z.

notes.checkAnswer: A neutral atom of ²³₁₁Na has 11 protons, 11 electrons and 12 neutrons.

notes.title: Isotopes, radioactivity and their uses
notes.answer: Isotopes are atoms of the same element with different numbers of neutrons. Their chemical properties are almost the same, while their physical properties may differ.
notes.explanation: Isotopes have the same number of protons and electrons but different numbers of neutrons. Their electron arrangements are the same, so their chemical behaviour is almost the same; their different masses can give them different physical properties.
notes.simple: Isotopes are atoms of the same element with different numbers of neutrons. They react almost alike, but their different masses can make some physical properties different.
examples: ¹²₆C and ¹⁴₆C are isotopes of carbon: each has 6 protons, but they have 6 and 8 neutrons respectively.
Tritium, ³₁H, is radioactive; hydrogen, ¹₁H, and deuterium, ²₁H, are stable.
steps: Find the element's atomic number: this gives the number of protons.
For a neutral atom, the number of electrons equals the number of protons.
Find neutrons by subtracting the atomic number from the mass number.
For a relative atomic mass, multiply each isotope's mass by its percentage abundance, add the results, and divide by 100 when the abundances are percentages.
notes.checkQuestion: Why can isotopes of the same element have different masses?
notes.checkAnswer: Isotopes have the same number of electrons, so they show almost the same chemical behaviour. Their different numbers of neutrons give them different masses and physical properties.

notes.title: Calculating Relative Atomic Mass
notes.explanation: An element’s relative atomic mass is the weighted average of the masses of its isotopes, using their percentage abundances.
notes.simple: Multiply each isotope’s mass by its percentage abundance, add the results, then divide by 100.
examples: For krypton, the relative atomic mass is 83.7.
For chlorine, the relative atomic mass of the light isotope is 34.95.
steps: Multiply each isotope mass by its percentage abundance.

notes.title: Atomic structure, isotopes and radioactivity
notes.explanation: Atomic structure explains how protons, neutrons and electrons are arranged, why elements differ, and how isotopes and radioactivity behave.
notes.simple: An atom has a tiny nucleus containing protons and neutrons, with electrons arranged around it. The number of protons identifies the element.
examples: A neutral oxygen-16 atom has 8 protons, 8 electrons and 8 neutrons.
A neutral bismuth-210 atom has 210 − 83 = 127 neutrons.
steps: Read the atomic number: it gives the number of protons.
For a neutral atom, set the number of electrons equal to the number of protons.
Subtract the atomic number from the mass number to find neutrons.
For relative atomic mass, multiply each isotope mass by its abundance and find the weighted mean.
